alalal-c48145-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 20: whether every change takes place in place or in time.

alalal-c48145-d1e113.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's (Augustine's) statement that change happens in two ways, by place or by time.

alalal-c48145-d1e125.summary: Remarks that these two modes seem to have been taken without technical precision, introducing objections.

alalal-c48145-d1e133.summary: First objection: there is no motion of time, since time is neither motion nor its subject but a property; so not everything moved is moved in time.

alalal-c48145-d1e146.summary: Second objection: time is per se a property of local motion, and relates to other motions only as number and measure, so it should not be set against local motion as a separate mode.

alalal-c48145-d1e166.summary: Third objection: time is divided into parts taken from local motion, months, days and years, not from the parts of alteration or growth; so the division means nothing.

alalal-c48145-d1e186.summary: Solution: Augustine takes motion broadly here, as distinguished by the potency of the moveable for motion in any way.

alalal-c48145-d1e199.summary: Explains: motion is distinguished either by its terminus, as the six species of motion, or by its subject, as potency to 'where' only, as in the heavens, or to 'where' and form, as in elements. Augustine's division follows the latter: some things have potency to place, as every body of itself (said with an eye to the empyrean, which some hold immobile), others only to the succession of some form, and the time measuring that succession is prior by nature and understanding to local motion and its time. This removes the objections; the nature of that time is treated elsewhere.
claims: Augustine's division of change by place and time distinguishes potency to place from potency to succession of form, and the time measuring the latter is prior to local motion.
concepts: potency to ubi and to form

alalal-c48145.summary: Article 20 examines Augustine's claim, cited by Lombard, that all change happens by place or by time. Objections note that time is a property and measure of local motion, not a separate mode of change. Albert answers that motion is taken broadly here and distinguished by the potency of the subject. Some things have potency to place, as bodies do; others only to the succession of form, as in spiritual creatures. The time measuring such succession is prior by nature and understanding to local motion and its time.
claims: Augustine distinguishes change in place, based on potency to 'where', from change in time, based on succession of form.
The time measuring change of form is prior to local motion and its time.
